title: Scrubbers
ends: The vent stack is clean on your watch.

steps.q: HCl gas comes off a reactor vent. Which scrubbing liquid is the usual choice?
steps.title: Pick the liquid
steps.summary: HCl is very soluble in water, so a water stage absorbs most of it, producing weak acid that may be reusable, and a second stage with dilute caustic soda neutralises the remainder. In general, scrub acid gases with alkali and alkaline gases with acid.

draw: acid gas → alkali; alkaline gas → acid

steps.q: How much caustic soda (100 % basis) neutralises 100 kg of HCl?
steps.title: Caustic needed
steps.summary: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O, one mole each. With molecular weights of 36.5 and 40, 100 kg of HCl needs about 110 kg of NaOH on a 100 % basis, or about 1100 kg of 10 % solution. Neutralisation releases about 13.7 kcal per mole and dissolving gaseous HCl about 18 kcal per mole more, so a large HCl surge can make the liquor very hot.

steps.q: The scrubber outlet still shows acid fumes. Flow is fine, but half the packing looks dry. Why?
steps.title: Wet the packing
steps.summary: Gas absorption happens on wetted packing; dry packing does nothing. A blocked or tilted distributor, or a tall bed without redistribution, lets liquid channel down one side while gas rises through the dry side unscrubbed. Clean and level the distributor and fit redistributors every few metres in tall beds.

steps.q: When should the caustic in a scrubber be changed?
steps.title: Spent caustic
steps.summary: Caustic soda turns into salt as it reacts, so the scrubber liquor's pH falls with use. Below a certain pH it can no longer hold the gas and breakthrough occurs. Set a limit (often around pH 10, or better, a free-caustic titration), check it every shift or online, and start large acid-gas steps with fresh caustic.

opts.t: At its pH or strength limit

steps.q: Ammonia comes off a vent. Which scrubbing liquid suits it?
steps.title: Alkaline gases
steps.summary: Ammonia is alkaline, so it is scrubbed with dilute sulphuric acid, forming ammonium sulphate that stays in solution. Water alone absorbs ammonia but loses effectiveness as it loads and warms. Control an acid scrubber on pH too; its pH rises as the acid is consumed, so change it at the upper limit.

draw: water alone: weakens as it loads
acid scrubber: pH rises as it works

steps.q: The scrubber circulation pump trips while a reaction is giving off HCl. What should happen?
steps.title: Scrubber trips
steps.summary: If the scrubber circulation pump trips, the packing dries and gas passes straight through. Interlock low scrubber flow, or the pump, to stop the dosing or heating that generates the gas, add low-flow and low-pH alarms, and test the interlocks regularly.

opts.t: Keep dosing, the gas will wait
An interlock stops the gas-making step
Restart the pump later, after the batch

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Today: scrubbers, the last stop before a vent gas reaches the sky. Six questions. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Now try the packed scrubber calculator.

q1.text: Question 1. HCl gas comes off a reactor vent. Which scrubbing liquid is the usual choice?

q1-r0.text: HCl doesn't dissolve well in toluene. You'd just make a solvent vent.

q1-r1.text: Yes! Water takes the bulk, caustic polishes.

q1-r2.text: Acid won't neutralise an acid gas. Wrong team.

q1-r3.text: HCl to atmosphere? The neighbours, and the board, will object.

q1-b0.text: HCl dissolves very readily in water. A water stage takes most of it, and gives weak acid you may reuse.

q1-b1.text: A second stage with dilute caustic soda neutralises what's left.

q1-b2.text: Match the liquid to the gas: alkali for acid gases, acid for alkaline ones.

q1-b3.text: Very soluble or fast-reacting gases scrub well in short columns.

q2.text: Question 2. How much caustic soda (100 % basis) neutralises 100 kg of HCl?

q2-r0.text: That's half what you need. Check the molecular weights.

q2-r1.text: Close, but NaOH is a bit heavier per mole than HCl.

q2-r3.text: Twice too much. It's one to one.

q2-b0.text: HCl plus NaOH gives NaCl and water. One mole each.

q2-b1.text: HCl is 36.5, NaOH is 40. So each kilogram of HCl needs about 1.1 kilograms of caustic.

q2-b2.text: As 10 percent solution, that's about 1100 kilograms of liquid, plus a margin, since you change it before it's all used.

q2-b3.text: Neutralisation releases about 13.7 kilocalories per mole, and dissolving the gas adds about 18 more. A big HCl surge can make the liquor very hot.

q3.text: Question 3. The scrubber outlet still shows acid fumes. Flow is fine, but half the packing looks dry. Why?

q3-r0.text: Too much liquid floods. Yours isn't even wetting it.

q3-r1.text: Yes! Liquid channels down one side and gas sneaks up the dry side.

q3-r2.text: If it were clean, there'd be no fumes.

q3-r3.text: New packing works fine, if it's wet.

q3-b0.text: Absorption happens on the wet packing surface. Dry packing does nothing.

q3-b1.text: A blocked or tilted distributor, or no redistributor in a tall bed, lets liquid run down one side.

q3-b2.text: Gas takes the dry path, the easy way up, and leaves without being scrubbed.

q3-b3.text: Clean and level the distributor. Tall beds need a redistributor every few metres.

q4.text: Question 4. When should the caustic in a scrubber be changed?

q4-r0.text: A busy week can use it up in days. Go by the reading, not the calendar.

q4-r1.text: Colour won't tell you the strength.

q4-r2.text: Yes! Follow the pH, change at the limit.

q4-r3.text: It turns into salt water as it works. Forever is optimistic.

q4-b0.text: As caustic soda reacts, it turns into salt. The pH falls batch by batch.

q4-b1.text: Below a certain pH, the scrubber can't hold the gas any more. Breakthrough.

q4-b2.text: So set a limit, often around pH 10, or better, check the free caustic strength by titration, every shift or with an online meter.

q4-b3.text: Before a big HCl step, start with fresh caustic. Don't start a batch on spent liquor.

q5.text: Question 5. Ammonia comes off a vent. Which scrubbing liquid suits it?

q5-r0.text: Caustic and ammonia are both alkaline. No reaction, no scrubbing.

q5-r2.text: Correct! Acid grabs the ammonia and holds it as a salt.

q5-r3.text: Ammonia is toxic and smells terrible. Scrub it.

q5-b0.text: Ammonia is alkaline, so it needs an acid to hold it.

q5-b1.text: Dilute sulphuric acid turns it into ammonium sulphate, which stays in solution.

q5-b2.text: Water alone absorbs ammonia too, but it loses its grip as the solution builds up and warms.

q5-b3.text: Again, control on pH. Here the pH rises as the acid is used, so change it at the upper limit.

q6.text: Question 6. The scrubber circulation pump trips while a reaction is giving off HCl. What should happen?

q6-r0.text: Gas doesn't wait. It goes straight out of the vent.

q6-r2.text: That just sends more HCl outside, faster.

q6-r3.text: After the batch, the gas is already out.

q6-b0.text: Without circulation, the packing dries out and the gas goes straight through.

q6-b1.text: So interlock the scrubber flow, or the pump, to the dosing or heating that makes the gas.

q6-b2.text: Alarm on low flow and low pH too, so the operator knows before fumes reach the stack. A standby pump that starts by itself helps, because gas can keep coming after dosing stops.

q6-b3.text: Test those interlocks regularly. Check your scrubber with the packed scrubber calculator on pharmacheme dot in.
